General Motors on Thursday reported a year-over-year sales decline of 5.5%, with 670,974 new vehicles sold during the third quarter.
GM's sales of all-electric vehicles are down across the board, as enthusiasm for EVs wanes. EV demand spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending up to $7,500 in federal incentives for consumers to purchase an electric vehicle. During the same period last year, GM reported record sales of its electric vehicles.
Against those comparisons, EVs this year saw dramatic drops, with the Equinox EV down 92.4% during the most recent quarter, at 1,905 vehicles sold. The Blazer EV was down 84.4% and Hummer EV sales fell 72.9%.
The report comes after Cox Automotive said last week that new vehicle sales have been stronger than expected this year and raised its 2026 forecast by roughly 2%, to 16.1 million units.
Hybrid vehicle sales are expected to capture a growing market share of car sales, as inflated gas prices pressure consumers.
Despite offering a broad EV lineup, the Detroit automaker only offers one hybrid vehicle, a Corvette. Experts expect GM's weakness in the sector to impact its overall sales.
Hybrids assisted other automakers in outperforming GM in third-quarter sales.
Toyota Motor reported that its EV and hybrid vehicles made up over 57% of the Japanese automaker's sales this quarter.
Toyota said sales were up 0.6% for the most recent quarter, with 633,223 vehicles sold. Sales of its electrified vehicles, which include hybrids, were up 28.5%, with 363,367 units sold.
That helped Toyota continue to narrow its gap with U.S. sales leader GM, which is now less than 136,000 units. That compares to a full-year gap of roughly 335,000 units last year.
Cox Automotive earlier this year said if such sales trends continue, Toyota could once again overtake GM to become the U.S. sales leader in the coming years.
Honda Motor, which also offers several hybrids and leads major automakers in fuel economy in the U.S., reported a 9.3% increase in U.S. third-quarter sales. Its hybrid sales were a record of more than 106,000 units during the quarter.
"We've got really high demand for hybrids," Lance Woelfer, head of American Honda Motor's U.S. sales, told CNBC. "We're finding more and more consumers are figuring out hybrids meet their needs."
High fuel prices, with an AAA national average of $4.41, were also expected to impact sales of big trucks and SUVs, sectors that GM relies on. GM's full-size pickups were relatively flat.
Each of the automaker's brands are down so far year to date, led by a 25% decline in Cadillac.
GM's lower-cost vehicles are a bright spot for the company as consumers face high inflation. The Chevrolet Trailblazer was up 51% for the third quarter, while sales of Buick Envista were up 18.4% and Chevrolet Trax up 16.3%.
Despite falling sales, Duncan Aldred, president of GM North American, remained optimistic.
"Our business is performing very well, the launch of our next-generation full-size pickup trucks is on track, and we are making investments in new vehicles, innovative technologies, and our U.S. manufacturing footprint to drive our next phase of growth," Aldred said in a statement .
General Motors last month announced additional details about its new V-8 engines for its pickup trucks, as it attempts to maintain leadership in truck sales.

articles.title_zh: DC judge permanently dismisses case charging ex-Olympian with vandalizing Reflecting Pool
articles.content_orig:
Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, left, and his attorney Norm Eisen, right, leave D.C. court with a smile in early September after a hearing about the dismissal of his vandalism charges. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.
In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.
Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury , though he pleaded not guilty .
In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.
Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."
Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.
When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.
Hearn's supporters rally outside the District of Columbia Courthouse during an early September hearing. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.
Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."
The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga , which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.
In an August interview with NPR , Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.
"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.
Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."
"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.
"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August , in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.
It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.
Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.
The empty, fenced-off Reflecting Pool as seen in late September. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"
He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."
"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.
Hearn's lawyers say Thursday's ruling allows him "to move forward with his life as he deserves."
The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

The world's largest thoroughbred auction broke records this year despite concerns that the Gulf conflict would deter deep-pocketed racehorse buyers from the Middle East.
The Keeneland September Yearling Sale in Kentucky grossed $536.7 million this year, surpassing last year's record by about $5 million. At the two-week auction, which ended Sept. 26, 70 yearlings sold for at least $1 million, up from 56 last year, which broke a 19-year record. The average yearling price increased nearly 7% to $187,933.
The top lot, a dark bay colt with white socks, was bought for $3.7 million, by a group of investors including paper mogul Peter Brant. The colt was sired by champion stallion Into Mischief, who has produced three Kentucky Derby winners.
Horse breeder and accountant Len Green said tax breaks from the "one big beautiful bill" was an important driver of the strong auction results in recent years. At last year's September Sale , which took place two months after OBBBA was signed into law, sales jumped 24% from the year prior.
"If you happen to be successful and you wanted to have something that gives you a tax deduction and gives you publicity, taking pictures and being in newspapers, et cetera, that kind of thing, the horse business is a pretty damn good investment to make," Green said.
OBBBA permanently reinstated 100% bonus depreciation, a tax incentive that allows businesses to write off qualified business property. While bonus depreciation is more commonly associated with commercial real estate and private jets, businesses can write off 100% of a racehorse purchase in the first year of ownership. Racehorse owners can get more bang for their buck by writing off related assets like riding equipment and barns or forming an LLC, Green added.
He added that while the stock market and private-equity exits have created massive wealth, owning a sports team is still out of reach for many entrepreneurs. The racehorse industry has a much lower price of admission, he said.

Shannon Arvin, president and CEO of Keeneland, pointed to other factors, including higher purses in many racing jurisdictions.
Buyers from the Middle East, including members of the ruling families of Dubai and Qatar, have become a prominent presence at the top-end of the thoroughbred market.
Before the auction, Arvin thought it was possible that the Gulf conflict would deter Middle East buyers. However, it did not appear to impact attendance, she said.
"We always kind of hold our breath until they get here," she said. "But there wasn't anybody that we're aware of that didn't come because of the conflict."
Arvin said about a quarter of yearlings were purchased by international buyers, including from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Libya. Keeneland does not break out specific numbers by country.
The biggest buyer at the auction was a newly formed partnership of four racing partnerships and owners, spending $16.2 million on 20 horses combined. While partnerships have become more popular, they haven't reduced sales in the way that was once feared, Arvin said.
"What we've actually seen is that these partnerships, because people are joined up, they tend to spend more," she said. "It lets them diversify their investment and have more opportunities for success. And what I found in talking to a lot of those buyers that decide to buy in partnership is that they love the camaraderie of buying with others, of buying with their friends."

South Korea's $200 billion investment into the U.S., which President Donald Trump said would transform America "for generations," is not a done deal in totality.
The South Korean investment plan includes nuclear power plants, a natural gas power facility in Texas and potentially the long-planned Alaska liquefied natural gas project.
Trump in a Truth Social post late Wednesday stateside said the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion, drawing a response from South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, who emphasized that involvement in some of the projects remains subject to commercial considerations.
Lee in an X post on Thursday local time said that participation in the Alaska LNG project was dependent on its financial viability and legal compliance. He added that investments in nuclear power plants would also require assessment of commercial viability on a plant-by-plant basis.
Trump had hailed South Korean investments in his post late Wednesday stateside, saying that the countries had agreed to work on the Alaska LNG project, pegging its value at $50 billion.
The joint statement earlier Wednesday, however, had mentioned that work on the project was contingent on "commercial reasonableness," without highlighting details on allocations toward the project.
The Alaska LNG project seeks to transport natural gas roughly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from fields on Alaska's North Slope to the southern part of the state, where it would be liquefied for export to markets including Asia, reported Yonhap. The project has faced long-standing questions over its economics given the large up-front investment required.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan had described it as "high-risk" last year and said participation would be difficult unless it could generate sufficient cash flow.
Overall, the investment package includes $22.3 billion for a 6,472-megawatt natural gas power facility in Encinal, Texas, that will supply electricity to co-located data centers. The project will be led by developer Related Cos. and U.S. power company NextEra Energy , with the first phase expected to begin commercial operations in 2029 and the full facility coming online in stages by 2032.
Trump said the investments would turn South Korea's commitments into "huge construction projects" and create "tens of thousands of American jobs."
"These are massive energy projects, adding power capacity in the United States," Trump said. "This is new construction, new manufacturing, and great jobs for American workers."
The two countries said they would seek to expand Korean companies' participation in the Texas project across equipment supply, engineering and construction as well as long-term operations and maintenance. The U.S. also intends to give Korean companies opportunities to supply equipment, including turbines, to similar projects in the country.
Another $120 billion has been allocated to plans for eight large-scale nuclear reactors in the U.S. Of that amount, $100 billion is earmarked for construction costs and $20 billion for contingency reserves.
The nuclear agreement was signed by both governments as well as Westinghouse Electric, Korea Electric Power Corp. and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power. The plan also calls for pursuing a potential significant minority investment in Westinghouse by Korean companies, with the terms subject to commercial negotiations.

Public frustration over the economy and rising prices is weighing heavily on President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, with a majority of Americans blaming his policies for stubbornly high costs.
Just 17% of US adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his management of the broader economy, according to a new Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
Nearly two-thirds, 65%, say Trump's policies are primarily responsible for high prices rather than factors outside his control, amid frustration over tariffs and the war with Iran.
The findings come weeks before midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Trump has been campaigning heavily for Republicans, but dissatisfaction has spread to some of his own supporters.
"I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker and Republican from Bradford, Pennsylvania.
"He said, ‘Make America Great Again.’ And I have not seen him do that."
Concern about everyday expenses has risen sharply. About half of Americans say they are "extremely" or "very" concerned about affording gasoline, up from 39% in July, while a similar share are highly concerned about food costs.
"Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel," said Pedro Sanchez, 52, a California law enforcement worker who voted for Trump. "I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more."
Trump's economic approval has fallen 14 percentage points since March 2025. About 7 in 10 Americans say his handling of living costs has been worse than expected, including roughly half of Republicans.
About 6 in 10 Republicans now disapprove of Trump's handling of living expenses, up from about half in April, although 67% of Republicans still blame high costs primarily on factors outside his control.
The poll also found growing dissatisfaction with Trump's foreign and trade policies. Some 69% of Americans say the war with Iran has not been worth fighting, while just 28% approve of Trump's handling of Iran.
Only about 3 in 10 approve of his handling of international trade, and 64% say he has gone too far with new tariffs.
Overall, about 3 in 10 Americans approve of Trump's performance as president, while roughly 6 in 10 say the country is worse off than when his second term began. Border security remains his strongest issue, with about half approving of his performance.
Trump's economic approval is now comparable to President Joe Biden's 28% rating in June 2022 during pandemic-era inflation. But Americans were less likely to directly blame Biden at the time: in October 2022, 44% said his policies were responsible for high prices, compared with 65% who now blame Trump's policies.
Sanchez said Trump's tariffs and the Iran war had directly contributed to his disappointment.
"I think he has a lot to do with it," he said. "I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control."

Everyone knows what happens in Carrie . Fifty-two years after its publication, the novel that ignited Stephen King ’s career has so thoroughly engulfed the culture, you’d have to be almost as sheltered as Carietta White herself not to have absorbed its most indelible images. The locker-room tampon gauntlet and “Plug it up!” chant. Carrie’s smothering holy-roller mom, locking her up in prayer-closet solitary confinement. The eerily unlikely prom date. The swinging bucket that has haunted every coronation of school-dance royalty in film and TV since Brian De Palma first adapted the book in 1976.
It’s a tale as old as time: Warped by her mother’s zealotry and scapegoated since childhood by her classmates, 16-year-old Carrie has a late, traumatic menarche that reactivates her latent telekinetic abilities. Then, after accepting a pity date to the prom, she’s crowned queen and immediately gets pig’s blood dumped on her head by a resentful bully. The humiliation causes her to lay waste to the school and then the town, using her powers to exact revenge.
Sissy Spacek in Carrie (1976) Getty
King’s book and De Palma’s film became classics of the horror genre. No less venerable a critic than Pauline Kael wrote of Sissy Spacek’s Oscar-nominated portrayal: “I don’t see how this performance could be any better.” Yet in the 21st century, new interpreters keep trying to improve upon it. With platforms scrambling to capitalize on popular IP, it’s no mystery why this would sound like a good idea to Hollywood executives. But something else must be inspiring high-minded filmmakers like Boys Don’t Cry director Kimberly Peirce, who released a divisive remake in 2013, to keep resurrecting Carrie .
The fourth screen adaptation of the novel (unless you count the pitiful 1999 sequel, The Rage: Carrie 2 ) is an eight-episode Prime Video series created by Mike Flanagan , who is known both for riffing on horror touchstones in Netflix hits like The Haunting of Hill House and The Fall of the House of Usher and for his features based on King novels like Gerald’s Game and Doctor Sleep . Premiering Oct. 7, his ambitious Carrie is the first that manages to fully get out from under the shadow of De Palma’s. Yet it confirms a gradual shift in how the story is being told. What was once an account of an abusive mother and an evil bully unwittingly uniting to create a lethal monster has become, with each new incarnation, more like an indictment of society as a whole.
Summer H. Howell, left, and Samantha Sloyan in Carrie (2026) Liane Hentscher—Prime
All three Carrie movies are mostly faithful to the novel, dutifully reproducing every major plot point and set piece, as well as a lot of dialogue. King’s writing is remarkably cinematic, which is probably why he’s our most adapted living author . But every Carrie is also a product of its time. De Palma, whose masterfully crafted version turns 50 in November, seems to lust after and fear the female body in equal measure—a common response within what was then a male-dominated genre to the feminist upheavals of the ’70s. It’s hard to imagine a contemporary adaptation pairing its opening credits with a steamy, slow-motion parade of nude high school girls in their locker room. A 2002 made-for-TV movie written by cult creator Bryan Fuller ( Hannibal ) is a relic of an era when the only things teen girls loved more than low-rise denim were movies where female misfits get glow ups ( She’s All That , 10 Things I Hate About You , Jawbreaker ). Just over a decade later, Peirce incorporated smartphones and YouTube, as well as an emerging pop-feminist sensibility that traced the derangement of Carrie’s mom, Margaret (played here by Julianne Moore ), to childbirth trauma and found a palpably empowered Carrie actively choosing who to kill and who to save.
You can find support for each of these readings in King’s own reflections. “The book is, in its more adult implications, an uneasy masculine shrinking from a future of female equality,” he wrote in his 1981 nonfiction book Danse Macabre . “For me, Carrie White is a sadly misused teenager, an example of the sort of person whose spirit is so often broken for good in that pit of man- and woman-eaters that is your normal suburban high school. But she's also Woman, feeling her powers for the first time and, like Samson, pulling down the temple on everyone in sight.” In her influential 1992 study Men, Women, and Chain Saws: Gender in the Modern Horror Film , the scholar Carol J. Clover suggests that this tangle of intentions explains the broad and, in some ways, contradictory appeal of Carrie across genders. Its protagonist is, at once, a projection of female power and male fear and the universal horror of bullying.
Despite feeling mostly redundant, the two features released after Clover’s book shared a new emphasis. De Palma’s stylish ’70s chiller played up the ghoulishness of Margaret (a bellowing, vicious Piper Laurie) and of Carrie’s chief tormentor at school, the sadistic mean girl Chris Hargensen (Nancy Allen), as well as the otherworldly oddness of Spacek’s lead. But Fuller’s and especially Peirce’s films sand down those characters’ excesses, revealing motivations and vulnerabilities that make them harder to hate or fear. (The latter faced criticism for casting the conventionally beautiful, preternaturally confident Chloë Grace Moretz in the title role.) At the same time, we see the condescending assumptions behind the actions of ostensibly heroic figures like Sue Snell, the popular girl who tries to atone for hazing Carrie by sending her boyfriend to the prom with her. In these movies, Carrie’s reign of terror is the ultimate expression of the school’s brokenness. As the critic Matt Zoller Seitz wrote in a favorable review of the 2013 version: “The first Carrie was horror. This is tragedy.”
Bullies face off against their prey in Carrie (2026) Prime
If the 21st century Carrie movies spoke to a post-Columbine era of school shootings , then Flanagan’s series is a product of the Trump decade, in which seemingly every aspect of American life has fractured along bipartisan political lines. The educational realm has become a crucible for debates around censorship , technology , parental rights , gun control , LGBTQ inclusion , critical race theory , the teaching of science vs. religion , social media . Which explains how Flanagan and his creative team, which includes many female writers and directors, found in this slight story eight episodes’ worth of material.
Without omitting any of the moments King fans will anticipate, they depart pretty boldly from the text. This Carrie opens with the death of Carrie’s conspiracy-theorist father (who, in previous versions, she never got to know) in a bizarre accident on his construction site. Somehow, no one knows he had a wife (Flanagan regular Samantha Sloyan, locating the wounded soul of a character who’s always been more of a caricature) and daughter (a movingly fragile Summer H. Howell) until they’re found cowering at home, in the closet where they pray. The previously homeschooled Carrie is forced to enroll at the local public high school while Margaret gets a job at a soulless big-box store, where her refusal to ring up a sex toy gets her demoted to cleaning toilets.

articles.title_orig: What a Pearly King taught me about Cockney rhyming slang and East London history
articles.title_zh: What a Pearly King taught me about Cockney rhyming slang and East London history
articles.content_orig:
George Major, known as the Pearly King of Peckham, wears his blinged-out suit in 2024. He died in August at age 88. Tony Kershaw/Getty Images hide caption
LONDON — He was one of my most memorable interviews. Even though we were both speaking English, I could barely understand a word he was saying.
"The costermongers, wheeze used to fly-pitch, on this frog and toad," he said — at least I think, after listening to my tape several times again, none the wiser.
Our interview was back in 2016, on one of my first NPR reporting trips to London. George Major, then 78, was a local celebrity. We walked together through the East End, where the factories and docklands that Major grew up around during World War II have given way to glass skyscrapers. A vendor ran out into the street to slap him high-five. Tourists snapped photos.
Major had turned up in bling: A black suit and flat cap, both festooned with sequins, sparkles and mother-of-pearl buttons. His title — Pearly King of Peckham — was spelled out in shimmering buttons across the back of his jacket.
He was a charming wheeler-dealer. But his language — a mix of what he called "backspeak" and Cockney rhyming slang — was impossible for this hapless American visitor to understand.
At one point in our video interview, I glanced at the camera and exclaimed, "We might need a translator here!"
Ten years later, I chuckle whenever I land at Heathrow Airport, where a portrait of Major covers an entire wall. But this summer, a former colleague alerted me to an item in the local press, which hit me harder than I expected: The Pearly King of Peckham died Aug. 1, aged 88.
He was buried Sept. 14 in a cemetery not far from the Cockney Museum he founded. A horse-drawn cart carried his casket into a little chapel, whose walls shook with mourners singing raucous pub songs. One of the gardeners outside looked bewildered.
At the gravesite, I approached the Major family, offered condolences, and hesitantly shared the story of my brief, confusing 2016 encounter with their loved one.
A horde of pearly kings, queens, princes and princesses — four generations of Major's family, all in matching pearly suits — turned and looked at me, some through tears, then threw back their heads and laughed.
"A real Cockney cheeky chappy!" his daughter Janet Major said, hugging me.
Pearly kings and queens, wearing clothes decorated with mother-of-pearl buttons, are committed to raising money for charities. Laura Chiesa/LightRocket viz Getty Images hide caption
In the 1870s, an orphaned street sweeper named Henry Croft began decorating his suit with mother-of-pearl buttons scavenged from the streets outside textile factories that used to dot London's East End.
His pearly garb infused menial work with dignity — a royal air, even — and launched what would become a working-class East London institution: The pearly kings and queens .
"These pearly suits are now cultural artifacts with fantastic designs, telling a profound story about London and Cockneys, what we call the non-posh Londoners," says Andy Green, co-founder of the Modern Cockney Festival, an annual celebration of diverse, working-class communities in London.
Some of the so-called pearlies were street hawkers, market vendors or fly-pitchers — unlicensed traders. Others canvassed for charity. Many were immigrants, their slang peppered with words from Yiddish or Bengali. They became neighborhood fixtures, in mother-of-pearl finery.
"You had what are called costermongers, which is a posh word for street hawkers, street sellers," Green says. "Imagine you're a newly arrived immigrant in the country. One of the first jobs you could possibly do might be to hustle, sell goods on the street."
That's what George Major did. Born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, he was abandoned as a child, grew up in a workhouse , and found odd jobs in the local market as a teenager, his daughter Janet explains.
"Dad eventually became one of the costermonger kings that used to run market stalls," she says. "It was not an easy childhood, but he followed the ideals of Henry Croft. That was before the welfare state, when you had to help your friends, your neighbors, your community."
Janet Major describes the weekends of her childhood, with her father leading all seven of his children, walking door to door in matching pearly suits, asking for money for charity.
Nowadays, a dwindling number of pearlies still canvass for charities like children's hospitals, women's shelters and veterans groups. They appear at summertime street festivals and march in parades.
George Major later trained as a plumber and ran a plumbing supply shop, she says.
Onscreen, the pearly kings inspired the streetwise, heart-of-gold chimney sweep character of Bert in Walt Disney's Mary Poppins film — played by Dick Van Dyke, an American who later owned up to what he called "the most atrocious Cockney accent in the history of cinema."
The Major family and others believe George Major himself inspired another fictional character: Del Boy , the happy-go-lucky East London huckster in the long-running British sitcom Only Fools and Horses . He's a cheeky salesman, always scheming to get rich quick, with the catchphrase, "This time next year, we'll be millionaires!"
At his funeral, Major's eulogy was riddled with Del Boy quotes.
But like the TV protagonist, Major also broke the law. In 2012 he was sentenced to six months in prison, after pleading guilty to benefits fraud . He was released early.
"If he could avoid the tax man, he would!" his daughter laughs. "He used to say, 'Discount for cash!' He'd love a bargain."
His fame overshadowed his legal troubles. Major was one of dozens of pearly royals who marched in the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics.
George Major, seen here in 1975, was born in 1938 inside a military barracks in Peckham, southeast London, and grew up in a workhouse before he became the best-known pearly king of his generation. Chris Moorhouss/Hulton Archive via Getty Images hide caption
Years later, I finally figured out what Major meant back in 2016 when he told me he was a "costermonger" (street hawker) who used to "fly-pitch" (sell stuff without a license) on the "frog and toad" where we did our interview.
In Cockney rhyming slang, "frog and toad" means road. "Porky pies" means lies. "Apples and pears" means stairs. "Whistle and flute" means suit. "Ruby Murray" means curry. The vocabulary is extensive, and bewildering to outsiders — which is precisely the point. Green, the Cockney expert, says this type of slang likely originated as a code to confuse the police, or to secretly rig prices among street vendors.
To complicate things, Major also spoke in what he called "backspeak," sometimes also called backslang, which is even more confusing. One example that's crept into mainstream British slang is the word "yob" for boy. Take any word at all, and simply spell it backwards.
One of the only parts of that 2016 interview I could understand at the time was when Major waxed poetic about his family's unique pearly suit pattern. He pointed to a row of buttons on his sleeve, calling them "the line of life."
Ten years later, at his funeral, I found myself examining the same pattern on a pearly outfit worn by his great-granddaughter.
"There's a straight line, which is your life line," Aleisha Gordon, 19, said, pointing to a row of shimmering buttons. "The triangles are the ups and downs in life, and the flowers are the friends and family that help you along the way."
After the funeral, children threw handfuls of earth as George Major's coffin was lowered into the ground. The undertaker brought out four caged doves for Major's descendants to release skyward. The birds circled twice overhead, then disappeared.
People shared anecdotes about a "real rascal" and "the most hilarious person" who was nevertheless "very particular" about who made his tea. Someone turned on a boombox, and mourners began kicking their legs

articles.title_orig: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
articles.title_zh: Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
articles.content_orig:
Adam Polovincik on the Flydubai flight
A man has described how he hugged and reassured his two young children as their plane suddenly descended after one pilot stabbed the other in an attempt to seize control of the flight.
A Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes around two hours into its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered him and retook control to land safely.
Adam Polovincik told BBC Newshour that he hugged his six-year-old son and three-year-old daughter "really hard" and tried to stay calm for them as the attack unfolded.
He praised the pilot who was stabbed and passengers who fought off and subdued the attacker, saying they were "true heroes".
The stabbed pilot is in a stable condition in hospital, while the alleged attacker has been arrested.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to say whether Iran was involved in the attack , but that the alleged attacker had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
Polovincik, who was sitting in aisle 13, was flying home with his wife and children after an "amazing" holiday in Singapore and Thailand.
He said there had been a "huge degree of panic" on the plane as there was a "very, very, very sharp decrease in height".
What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel
He thought at first that this was simply because of an air pocket, but "it took a lot of time, almost a minute".
Everyone who had not been seated fell to the floor, the 40-year-old said.
"After a couple of seconds, we started to hear screams. 'There is blood, there is stabbing, we need help'," Polovincik said.
"At the end of the day, you understand very, very quickly that literally there is nothing that you can do at this point in time," he said.
Polovincik, a performance marketing analyst, said he tried to "be cool" for his children.
"You just tell them, yeah, everything's going to be all right. It's just a malfunction in the aeroplane, there is a crew under control, the passengers are helping them, [you] hug them really hard and try to keep your face so it doesn't look very panicked, try to keep your tone of voice."
But he said there was naturally a "high degree of panic" on the flight.
There were lots of families with children on the plane because the flight took place towards the end of a Jewish holiday period.
After about 10 to 15 minutes, he said a passenger in the cockpit told them the incident was "under control" and other staff were flying the plane.
In a video released by Netanyahu's office, passenger Yaniv Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out of the cockpit before other passengers helped pin him down.
Two other pilots who were onboard the flight then took over the controls and safely landed the plane, which had been carrying more than 150 passengers.
Polovincik said: "After they told us that the situation is, again, 'under control', then it was a bit harder to tell the kids that it's malfunctioned because people start to walk around the aeroplane covered with blood."
Polovincik was praised Indian pilot, Capt Smit Machchhar, who fought off his attacker and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing passengers to step in.
"Without him opening the door, we're probably not speaking here right now," he said, adding that he "can't even start saying our gratitude for this human being".
Polovincik said that, although he was not religious, he could not escape "the feeling that it was the hand of God yesterday" that had put "the pieces on the board in the way that they did".
After the situation onboard was brought under control, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where Polovincik stressed the passengers, who were almost all Israeli, were treated well.
"They brought us water and food and coffee and even sweets for the kids - even though we don't have any diplomatic relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia," he said.
The alleged attacker, who was arrested in Saudi Arabia, is expected to be transferred to the United Arab Emirates, from where the plane departed, Netanyahu told Fox News.
The passengers were taken to Tel Aviv on another flight later on Wednesday and were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
Polovincik said it had been "such a terrible ending" to an amazing family trip and that it would take some time for his family to come to terms with what had occurred.

articles.title_orig: Statement Written by Police in Cornell Assault Case Omitted Her Claim She Was Raped
articles.title_zh: Statement Written by Police in Cornell Assault Case Omitted Her Claim She Was Raped
articles.content_orig:
Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Wednesday in Ithaca, N.Y. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.
That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.
NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."
This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor, who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG on Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.
NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.
CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.
Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police, Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.
Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG on Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email that he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.
Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.
He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.
In mid-September, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.
Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.
Since Tuesday, Cornell has directed the public to an FAQ page on the rape allegations.
The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions. Cornell has not specified how many students faced punishments, or of what nature. It noted in the FAQ: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response."
WSKG found that as of Wednesday, the university has changed its FAQ. And it has quietly removed a sentence stating that the Cornell police "shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office."
Previously, the FAQ read: "The Cornell University Police Department investigated the matter in 2024 and shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
But by Wednesday afternoon , WSKG found that statement had been edited, and any mention of Cornell police sharing "all investigatory information" with the district attorney had disappeared from the page.
"The Cornell University Police Department is a unit of the university, and its officers are sworn Tompkins County deputy sheriffs whose duties include the enforcement of law and order on Cornell property," the new statement reads. "This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction."
WSKG reported that Cornell University did not respond to its questions about these changes.
Late Wednesday, the school confirmed to NPR that it is bringing in an outside counsel to hold an independent examination of the alleged gang rape.
University officials told NPR they have no further details about how the investigation will play out. Previously, Cornell strongly defended how it handled the case when Doe first reported the incident to school officials two years ago.
The move comes after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for the school to open an outside investigation. In a video posted on X , Hochul also said she's considering new legislation to tighten sexual assault laws across the state.
"While we have some of the toughest laws on sexual assault on college campuses right here in New York, I think we can do better," she said. "This culture has to stop. And it will stop here in the state of New York."
WSKG's Aurora Berry contributed reporting.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices
The number of people applying for US unemployment benefits dipped last week to the lowest level since mid-July as lay-offs remain low and most American workers enjoy job security.
The Labor Department said on Thursday that initial jobless claims ticked down to 197,000 from a revised 198,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped by 2,500 to 200,000.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for lay-offs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have mostly stayed below 220,000 – historically low.
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began February 28.

articles.title_orig: Rick Ross arrested after woman accuses rapper of strangling, hitting her at Miami Beach home
articles.title_zh: Rick Ross arrested after woman accuses rapper of strangling, hitting her at Miami Beach home
articles.content_orig:
Rapper Rick Ross was arrested Thursday in connection with a domestic violence incident at his Star Island mansion, where a woman accused him of repeatedly striking her and restricting her breathing during an altercation in August, according to Miami Beach police.
Ross, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, voluntarily surrendered to detectives at Miami Beach Police headquarters Thursday before being taken into custody, police said. He was booked into the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center at 6:10 a.m.
The 50-year-old rapper faces one felony count of battery by strangulation and one misdemeanor count of battery. According to Miami Beach police and the arrest affidavit, the charges stem from an alleged late August domestic violence incident at his residence on Star Island that was reported to police on Sept. 29.
The arrest affidavit says Ross and the alleged victim had been in a relationship for about a year and were living together at the time of the alleged incident.
The woman told investigators that on Aug. 28 she was awakened around 7:44 a.m. by Ross, who she said was angry because she had been tagged in a photo on Instagram. Police said Ross questioned her about whether she was lying to him and allegedly slapped her in the face.
Later that morning, according to the affidavit, Ross accused the woman of being involved with another person and continued questioning her while she was in a bathroom. The woman told police Ross struck her in the chest several times and restricted her breathing by grabbing and twisting the collar of the hoodie she was wearing.
The affidavit alleges Ross then grabbed the woman by her ponytail and slammed her against a wall before striking her in the face, causing a busted lip. The report states he then pushed her to the floor, turned on the shower and attempted to spray her with the shower head. The woman was eventually able to leave the bathroom and later gathered her belongings and left the residence after Ross left, according to the affidavit.
Police said the woman later provided detectives with a sworn statement and timestamped photographs of her injuries. Investigators also reviewed surveillance video from the residence that they said showed a friend arriving to pick her up and being turned away. According to the affidavit, Ross later posted a photo on his Instagram account showing the friend arriving at the property.
Ross denied the allegations in a video statement posted to his Instagram Stories around noon Thursday.
"First and foremost, I'm totally innocent of the fabricated allegations made against myself. I repeat, I am totally innocent with these fabricated allegations," Ross said. "I have such an amazing team, and I'm totally confident that these fabricated allegations will be laid to rest."
Earlier on Thursday, Ross' attorney, Bradley Horenstein, also denied the allegations against his client and urged the public not to rush to judgment as the case moves through the legal process.
"All I can say is that the allegations are false. He's innocent. Everything is going to come out," Horenstein told CBS News Miami. "We just ask that you allow the process to play out before rushing to judgment, because the truth will come in."
Ross appeared via Zoom in Miami-Dade bond court Thursday morning, where Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Mindy Glazer said she had reviewed the arrest report and found probable cause in the case.
During the hearing, Horenstein noted that Ross is a celebrity and asked that his client's release be expedited. The judge set Ross' bond at $4,000 on the battery by strangulation charge and $1,000 on the misdemeanor battery charge, for a total of $5,000.
Ross bonded out late Thursday morning.
Glazer also issued a stay-away order involving the alleged victim, identified in court by her initials. Ross was ordered to have no direct or indirect contact with the alleged victim, including through third parties, social media or other electronic means, and to stay away from the person's home, workplace or school.
Ross was also ordered to surrender any firearms and concealed weapons and was prohibited from possessing firearms. The judge also ordered him not to engage in criminal activity or use illegal drugs while the case is pending.
His arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.
Ross, a Miami-area native known for songs including "Hustlin'," has been a prominent figure in hip-hop for two decades.
Nikiya  Carrero contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.title_zh: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.content_orig:
Walmart is aiming to make it as easy as possible for its customers to find exactly what they want.
The retailer is leveraging three new tools tied to its digital shelf labels for both customers and store associates to better find products. It's the latest part of the company's push to modernize its technology and incorporate artificial intelligence into its business.
"We are people-led, tech-powered," said Greg Cathey, Walmart's senior vice president of digital transformation. "But the way we look at it is AI as a way to help associates do their job and free up time to allow them to invest in what they love to do most, which is spend more time with customers and their fellow associates."
The new feature for shoppers, called Shop to Light, allows customers to find specific products on the Walmart app, navigate to the correct aisle in the store and then flash the digital shelf label of the product to locate it. The retailer is now incorporating it widely following a pilot program.
That tool is also paired with Pick to Light and Stock to Light, which use the same capabilities to help store associates pick items for digital orders and stock products. All three features will be rolled out to stores companywide by the holiday season, Cathey said.
"This is a use case that customers have asked us for, associates have asked us for," Cathey said. "It gives them time back, and I think if you look at a lot of what we're trying to do, it's all around convenience and being able to help associates and customers free up that time to invest it where they want."
The rollout comes as convenience and speed — particularly in the delivery and pickup segments — have become critical pieces of Walmart's efforts to increase sales. While Walmart's business has grown steadily, and its e-commerce sales continue to soar, investor concerns about its comparable sales and revenue outlook weighed on its stock after its most recent earnings report in August.
Walmart stores carry roughly 120,000 items. Cathey said it's a priority for the company to provide that large range of products while making it easier for customers to locate precise items.
While the company does not publicly share any financial aspects of the program, Cathey said the new features at pilot stores allow associates and customers to have more time while shopping and stocking. The Shop to Light feature has already seen 5 million flashes from customers since it began rolling out to limited locations this summer.
He said these new features will be especially important as the retailer heads into the busy holiday season, and the company views them as "a big win" for time savings.
Walmart began using digital shelf labels, as opposed to paper labels, to allow automatic and systemwide price changes to be rolled out at once. The company currently has more than 4,300 stores with digital shelf labels, and expects them to be installed across the chain by the end of the year, according to Walmart.
He added that the label prices are changed overnight, when customers aren't in the store, and the system has human oversight as well to ensure it has "robust governance" and doesn't make mistakes. Currently, roughly 90% of the sections within the store have digital shelf labels, he said.
"We don't look at it as technology for technology's sake," Cathey said. "So we always have a human in the loop, and we're very focused on human judgment and their ability to make decisions."
Walmart has been investing in its technology to modernize the business on both the consumer-facing side and in internal operations.
It's rolled out an AI agent to help customers with shopping, automated its supply chain, invested in radio frequency identification tags and set the stage for agentic commerce as it embraces AI. It's also spent billions on modernizing its store locations.
On Walmart's most recent earnings call, its CEO, John Furner, said the company is seeing significant returns on its technology strategies, including its investments in AI.
"We believe AI will improve nearly every part of our business by making shopping better, and our associates' work easier," he said.
Still, digital shelf labels and the company's AI push have sparked backlash. They have raised concerns about dynamic pricing and fears that digital labels could lead to price surges or privacy issues with collecting shopping data from customers.
But in an open letter last week, Furner said the company is continuing to "price the product, not the person," adding the retailer does not plan to use customer information to set prices.
"Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won't change the price," Furner wrote.
Cathey, who's been in his position for nearly a year, said his biggest priority when taking over the role was to focus on accelerating the speed of the technology that Walmart uses while keeping human oversight.
Several state legislatures, including New Jersey, have passed measures to restrict digital shelf labels over pricing concerns. Walmart said it has the feature in all of its stores in New Jersey.
Walmart in a statement called the policy an "overreaction, as digital shelf labels are not a tool for surveillance pricing and are simply a modern way to display prices."
Walmart has also invested in drone delivery – which has come under similar scrutiny over privacy concerns – to deliver products to customers in as fast as 30 minutes. That delivery option is available in select states, including Texas and Florida.
Ultimately, Cathey said the new digital shelf label features are all part of the company's bigger goal to ensure that store associates have more time to help meet the individual needs of customers.
And while investors debate whether physical retail or e-commerce is more important to the company's business, Cathey said the new features show that both go hand in hand.
"It's not one or the other anymore. It's both," he said. "We don't look at it as a store or an e-commerce fulfillment. They're actually one and the same."

Facing new competition in the audiobook market from Spotify, Audible is turning to AI and other technology to enhance the listening experience. On Thursday, the Amazon-owned company introduced three new features that will allow listeners to explore a book’s characters, engage in interactive stories, and view additional imagery and bonus information about landmarks or places mentioned in the book.
If you’re thinking the last would be great for highlighting the different courts’ locations in Sarah J. Maas’ faerie realm of Prythian, I must disappoint you. The feature will first arrive in just one title for now, “The Cultural Tutor: A Modern Guide to History, Art and Philosophy in 49 Short Chapters” by Sheehan Quirke, which focuses on making culture more accessible by teaching about poetry, art, architecture, geography, and more in short lessons.
The other new features, a character guide and interactive stories, are also starting off fairly small.
With Audible’s October 1 release of its Audible Original “Dracula,” the character guide will help listeners keep track of the cast of characters in the book, something that’s harder to do when listening than when reading. (The Audible Originals label doesn’t necessarily signal that the content is original, as “Dracula” is not. It means Audible’s own studios have produced the audiobook, memoir, exclusive series, podcast, or performance.)
In “Dracula,” the character guide will display who’s speaking in real time directly on the player page so listeners don’t get lost. It will also provide spoiler-free character cards, which showcase the narrator behind the voice and their bio. Audible says users will later be able to interact with the guide to ask questions about the story as it unfolds.
Other audiobooks gaining access to the character guide include the Audible Original of George Orwell’s “1984” and the forthcoming Audible Original “Exoplanet” from writer Benjamin Percy and executive producer Andy Weir (author of “Project Hail Mary” and “The Martian”).
A third feature, interactive stories, will also come to “Dracula” and “Exoplanet.”
Here, the idea is to bring the listener into the story through a bonus experience in which they interact with a book’s character. Powered by generative AI, the feature lets listeners interact with Dracula’s servant, Renfield, in the new Audible Original.
The character will speak first, giving the listener a role, goal, and stakes, and the listener then responds in their own words. The character will react to what’s said in real time.
Audible says the creators are involved in the foundations of the interactive stories, so the stories stay grounded in what’s happening in the book. Or, in the case of something like “Dracula,” the stories are meant to stay faithful to the original creator’s vision.
The changes come as audiobook listenership and revenue grow , with U.S. sales reaching $2.43 billion in 2025. The increased demand can be chalked up to several factors, from the proliferation of the smartphone to people’s increasingly busy schedules that make sitting down to read a book feel like a luxury. One could probably also credit TikTok’s “BookTok” community for pushing reading more into the mainstream — something that’s reflected in the most popular audiobook genres , which overlap with BookTok’s interests in fiction, sci-fi, thrillers, and, of course, romantasy.
“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” said Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza in a statement about the launch. “We’re excited to build on these while working hand in hand with creators, because we know that more time spent with stories benefits everyone who helps bring them to life.”
The company says the features are currently in a beta test, and the plan is to expand to more titles over time.

articles.title_orig: Padres 4, Cubs 1: Farewell to 2026, and on to an uncertain 2027
articles.title_zh: Padres 4, Cubs 1: Farewell to 2026, and on to an uncertain 2027
articles.content_orig:
The Cubs barely showed up in San Diego.
If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
When the Chicago Cubs began the 2026 season 27-12, a stretch that included two 10-game winning streaks, many of us thought, “Hey — maybe this year can be something special.”
Well. You know what happened after that. A 10-game losing streak. Injuries. Guys not producing. The bullpen imploding multiple times. After 27-12, they were just 62-61 — one game worse than the Marlins over that span. Sheesh.
And then, a Wild Card Series in which the Cubs offense pretty much vanished. That’s the story of Game 2, a 4-1 loss to the Padres that eliminated the Cubs from the 2026 postseason, almost as if they weren’t even there to begin with.
I could end this recap right there, because what more is there to say, really?
Nevertheless, you come here for game recaps and since this was the last Cubs game of 2026, let’s look at what happened.
One pitch into the bottom of the first inning, the Cubs were already ahead of Game 1 because, well, Fernando Tatis Jr. did not hit Kevin Gausman’s first pitch out of the yard. So, progress?
That progress lasted one inning. In the second, Ty France doubled and stopped at third on a single by Jackson Merrill. Xander Bogaerts singled in France, with Merrill stopping at third, where he scored on a sacrifice fly by Ethan Salas. Incidentally, Salas, who won’t turn 21 until next June, became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a MLB postseason game, breaking the record set by Atlanta catcher Bob Didier in 1969.
The 2-0 score is where the game stayed until the top of the fourth, when the Cubs finally broke through onto the board for the first time in this series.
Seiya Suzuki hit a one-out single and Ian Happ walked.
Nico Hoerner’s single up the middle scored Suzuki to make it 2-1 [VIDEO].
So, down by only one run in the fourth inning, with two runners still on base and only one out? Maybe the Cubs offense could get going here?
It was not to be, although after Matt Shaw struck out, Carson Kelly was hit by a pitch to load the bases.
Dansby Swanson flied to center to end the inning.
About that single run, from BCB’s JohnW53:
The Cubs did not score for the first 12.1 innings of this series.
That is the longest they ever have gone without scoring from the start of a post-season series. They were shut out in Game 1 of three previous series.
In the 1918 World Series vs. the Red Sox and 2015 Division Series vs. the Cardinals, they scored with one out in the second inning of Game 2.
In the 2016 World Series, they scored with one out in the first inning of Game 2.
The one-run deficit did not last long. Gausman struck out Merrill to start the fourth, but Bogaerts then doubled. Craig Counsell opted to bring in Daniel Palencia, who struck out Salas.
Then the Padres sent up Gavin Sheets to bat for Austin Hays. Sheets entered this game with career numbers of .297/.348/.484 with three home runs in 69 plate appearances against the Cubs during the regular season. You could have seen this coming all the way from San Diego to Chicago [VIDEO].
Palencia then hit Jake Cronenworth with a pitch, and the San Diego crowd booed as if that had been intentional; clearly, it was not — Palencia was just struggling with command.
The score might have been worse if not for this nice grab by Pete Crow-Armstrong off Tatis to end the inning [VIDEO] .
So at least we got a nice defensive memory from PCA from this series, even as his offense was silent — 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series.
That fourth inning was basically it. Palencia, David Peterson and Ryan Zeferjahn held the Padres scoreless the rest of the way, four combined shutout innings with four strikeouts. Meanwhile, the Cubs had just three more baserunners after the fourth. Michael Busch walked with two out in the fifth. Tyrone Taylor, batting for Busch, singled with one out in the eighth but was erased when Suzuki hit into a double play. Nico Hoerner doubled with one out in the ninth but was stranded. The Cubs went 1-for-8 with RISP in this game. If they’d hit in those situations would the result have been any different? I’m thinking probably not.
These two games in San Diego were a hallmark of this team, just as the offensive outbursts that had the 2026 Cubs lead MLB in runs also were. It was a real feast-or-famine season — long stretches where the offense could do no wrong, and others where the hitters just did not show up at all.
Here’s PCA on the season-ending loss [VIDEO].
Here are some postgame remarks from Alex Bregman [VIDEO].
Bregman, whose previous postseason performance was one of the reasons the Cubs signed him, went 0-for-8 in this series with four strikeouts.
Lastly, here are Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks [VIDEO].
Would the result of this series have been any different if the Cubs had won two more regular-season games and had home field? Probably not; it’s clear by watching these two games that the Padres were on a roll, which began over the last three weeks of the regular season and carried over into this series. Further, it’s very likely that weather would have been a major factor. It rained all day and evening in Chicago Wednesday and it’s still raining here early Thursday morning, which could have thrown scheduling for this series into chaos. In the end, this Cubs team just wasn’t good enough to move on, and you know the reasons, mostly pitching — injuries and ineffectiveness from both starters and relievers. The offense was great — until it wasn’t.
More on the offense from John:
In the two games of this series, the Cubs were 8 for 62, a batting average of .129. That is lower than in any of their 22 previous post-season series since 1901.
They batted .140 in the one-game Wild Card loss in 2018 and .145 in their two-game WC loss in 2020.
Other seasons below .200: .168 in 2017 (10 games) .181 in 1998 (3 games) .194 in 2007 (3 games) .196 in 1906 (6 games)
They batted .233 in 17 games when they won the World Series in 2016.
These are things that Cubs President of Baseball Operations Jed Hoyer will have to address this offseason, and that brings me to the upcoming uncertainty. Normally when a Cubs season ends, I’d tell you the next date we will see a Chicago Cubs team on the field the following year. They are scheduled to take the field Friday, Feb. 19, 2027 against the A’s at Ho Ho Kam Stadium in Mesa, Arizona. But with a looming owners’ lockout likely happening when the current MLB/MLBPA collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, there’s no guarantee that the 2027 Spring Training schedule — or regular season schedule — will be played as currently listed.
And so we wait. For developments, as is often said here.
In the meantime, stick around. We’ll have game threads here for all the remaining postseason games, including tonight’s decisive Phillies/Braves Game 3, which will begin at 7 p.m. CT (game thread will post at 6 p.m. CT). And of course, we’ll cover all the MLB offseason labor news and other baseball news here.
As is my custom, I will wrap my last game recap of the year by quoting from the late Commissioner Bart Giamatti’s “The Green Fields of the Mind” — quite appropriate today with the Chicago area weather.
It breaks your heart. It is designed to break your heart. The game begins in the spring, when everything else begins again, and it blossoms in the summer, filling the afternoons and evenings, and then as soon as the chill rains come, it stops and leaves you to face the fall alone. You count on it, rely on it to buffer the passage of time, to keep the memory of sunshine and high skies alive, and then just when the days are all twilight, when you need it most, it stops.
All of your communities in one place.

articles.title_zh: Amazon is launching colorful new Kindles — and a case with physical page-turn buttons
articles.content_orig:
A wave of little changes, including new colors, the option of an aluminum case, and some neat accessories.

Kindles don’t usually change much with each new version, but Amazon is launching next-generation models today that look and feel a whole lot nicer. The base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft are a millimeter thinner and 30 percent faster at opening books, and their power buttons have moved from the bottom to the right edge near the top.
They ship in vibrant new colors with a soft-touch plastic case, and, for the first time, there’s the option for a couple shades of aluminum, giving them a higher-end look and feel, not to mention double the storage of the plastic version (32GB versus 16GB). Amazon VP of Kindle Kevin Keith told The Verge that they all feature user-replaceable batteries to be in compliance with EU regulations , too.
The updated base Kindle is available today starting at $149.99 in a new purple color called ube and a plainer graphite color. It comes with 16GB of storage and lockscreen ads, and it looks nicer than the last-gen version, thanks to a seamless transition from frame to screen, moving on from the old design that had a recessed display.
New for this revision is the choice of aluminum , which bumps the price up to $189.99, doubles the storage, and ditches ads. The Kindle in aluminum is a very nice, compact thing to hold, especially in its new folio case that it can magnetically attach to. Though, at $239.98 all together ($189.99 for the e-reader and $49.99 for the case), you’re firmly in the territory of the Paperwhite, with its more pixel-dense and auto-dimming screen for $199.99 .
The display specs for the new Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (coming October 28th, available to preorder now) haven’t changed, though the color options have. The new plastic and aluminum colors available for each cover the entirety of the e-readers, not just their backsides. Amazon’s Keith credits a new technique of applying a black layer between the edges of the panel to prevent the case’s color from visually bleeding onto the screen.
The aluminum options for the Paperwhite and Colorsoft, costing $249.99 and $319.99 , respectively, include more than the base Kindle’s high-end version. These are the new Signature Edition versions, with pogo pins on their rear that are compatible with a $79.99 page-turn magnetic case that adds physical page-turning buttons a la the Kindle Oasis. Wireless charging isn’t offered in the new Signature Editions. Amazon will sell a $59.99 charging dock that can charge this edition upright and attaches via pogo pins.
Amazon is also adding a remote to the lineup, the Kindle Click. Amazon’s $34.99 Bluetooth remote lets you turn pages when you’re away from your device, with side-mounted buttons to adjust screen brightness. The remote’s main buttons are soft and quiet to press, and it’s lightweight, with a wrist strap to keep it from easily disappearing. It can recharge via USB-C, and it’s compatible with Kindles from 2024 or later.
Though we still seem be in the midst of Apple’s hardware launch season , Amazon has dropped a few new products so far in the past week, including a new Fire TV Stick 4K that can be powered directly through your TV’s USB port instead of requiring a power brick.

The horrors of modern high school loom large in Mike Flanagan’s “Carrie,” a series adaptation of Stephen King’s 52-year-old novel that’s keen to speak to today’s youth.
When Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) first enters Ewen P.H.S. after a lifetime of homeschooling, she’s greeted with metal detectors at the front doors, zombified students staring at their phones, and intrusive parents eager to contort curriculums on behalf of their kids. (Surprisingly, entitled adults aren’t even the most intrusive example of a damaged American psyche). On top of all that , she still has to handle classic teenage hardships like a tyrannical mother (although with this hormonal 16-year-old, any claims of having a certified wackjob for a mom would be accurate), nerd-induced ostracism (she loves to quote books that nobody but her teachers have read), and bullying — live in-person and via social media.
Entering a new school can feel like a lot to anyone, whether they’re raised in a traditional education system surrounded by friends, or learning math from Bible verses while isolated with doomsday-prepper parents. But Carrie stands out. She is, as a social worker says, “stunningly uninformed” — living her entire life without access to the internet, libraries, phones, or a community of disparate voices. Yet she’s also defiantly openhearted, even after her father dies at the start of our story. When the police arrive to break the news — finding Carrie and Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) hiding in a “prayer closet” — her mother’s irate fear is all but erased by Carrie’s elated smile. She’s not like her mom, and she’s not like the rest of us. She’s closer to an alien discovering Earth, as eager to explore as she is to turn strangers into friends.
But she’s also not like the rest of us — and kind of like some people’s idea of aliens — in that she can crush a car with her mind.
Within the genre staples and character beats familiar to fans of King’s novel (and Brian De Palma’s Oscar-nominated 1976 film), the 2026 version of “Carrie” loses its way. Carrie’s telekinesis leaks out in drips and drabs, as if Flanagan is as embarrassed by his lead character’s abnormality as a teenager trying to hide an acne flare-up. She rarely talks about her burgeoning ability, and aside from the inevitable, overdrawn, and underwhelming meltdown at prom, her superpower struggles to manifest into resonant frights.
But the horror is also hemmed in by one of the new “Carrie’s” core strengths: sympathy. Despite an opening montage in which a slew of witnesses debate whether Carrie is a victim or a bully, a hero or a monster, the series only sees her one way. It’s too timid to embrace evil, even as a temptation, and that limits its capacity to explore the human condition beyond mourning our collective lack of compassion.
As if there was any doubt, Flanagan’s adaptation extends an understanding embrace not just to Carrie, but her classmates, too. There’s Sue Snell (Siena Agudong), a friendly popular girl who’s dating “the hottest guy in school,” Tommy Ross (Joel Oulette), when she’s not hanging out with her best friend, Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton). While Tommy is Sue’s soulmate in kindness (quiet, sensitive, and unafraid to speak up for the unjustly maligned, he’s almost too good to be believed), Chris is a self-described “bitch” who promises to “never apologize for it.”
She never does, but she also doesn’t have to. “Carrie” does the apologizing for her, saddling Chris with a douchebag dad (Michael Trucco) so one-note he feels teleported in from a different show. While all the other characters show glimmers of decency, Mr. Hargensen’s disdain for his own daughter provides all the motivation Chris needs to vent her frustrations on the weird new girl, while every so often regretting how far her misplaced fury takes her. A locker room incident breeds resentment and mockery, before ballooning into further disputes that should prove familiar to anyone who attended a sizable school.
Chris is an instigator, but “Carrie’s” only real villains are adults. The series posits American society is letting down our kids and more specifically calls out parents for repressing, manipulating, and otherwise contaminating their natural nobilities. Unfortunately, the main representative of those messages is a mess.
Margaret White is a misanthrope and a hypocrite. She speaks down to everyone as if they only comprehend single-syllable words and rails against teachers for pushing an agenda in the same breath she uses to demand they enforce her will across the entire school. Her flaws are obvious, which makes her easy to root against, but her virtues, as few as they may be, don’t distinguish Margaret from Chris’ soulless father. She’s more controlling, sure, but she’s just as monotonous and predictable, which makes Carrie’s growing distrust in her own mother a tension-free wait for a foregone conclusion. With a little more development, Margaret could’ve been a complex, charismatic, and challenging force. Instead, she’s just a representative.
While “Carrie” lands closer to “The Midnight Club” than “Midnight Mass” in its showrunner’s oeuvre, it makes the most of Flanagan’s mesmeric monologues (even if some prove redundant), moves through its story smoothly (when it’s not planting seeds to extend beyond the book, the details of which I’m embargoed from bringing up), and features a slew of solid performances.
Some clunky plot maneuverings spare Howell the tricky heel turn you’d expect for the finale’s extended prom-tastrophe, but they allow the actor to settle into her affecting innocence. This version of Carrie could easily prove grating in the same way she does to her cynical tormentors — too oblivious, too sincere, too nice — but she’s always endearing, thanks in large part to Howell’s nuanced commitment to drawing out her awakening. Thornton is equally effective on the other end of the spectrum. As Chris succumbs to her worst instincts, you can appreciate her hesitancy as well as her relish, sometimes at the same time.
In scenes big and small, Flanagan’s trademark empathy is moving and earned, creating timely interpretations of age-old conflicts and eloquent emotional beats between characters in conflict. But it’s also flattening, for Carrie and for “Carrie.” The first season (of an intended three ) is attuned to its allegory about the horrors of high school, but it would never be confused with a horror show — not without its franchise baggage — and the imbalance makes for a teen drama that’s blunt, preachy, and broad.
Despite earnestly engaging with its younger characters while throwing the olds to the wolves, the series ultimately feels like it’s told from a parent’s perspective. It’s a plea instead of a roar, and the modern world, with all its problems, calls for screams.
