articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News Wednesday that the motive of the co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a passenger jet bound from Dubai to Tel Aviv was still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.
"I think it looks like a suicide attempt simply because of what this hero Yaniv described when he went in," Netanyahu speculated, referring to Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers on the FlyDubai flight who has been credited with entering the cockpit and helping to subdue the attacker.
"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said of the co-pilot, whose identity has not been revealed. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."
Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. In He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
According to Israeli officials, on Wednesday morning local time, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot stabbed the captain.
Per data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News, the plane then plunged about 17,000 feet, climbed 5,000 feet, and then fell another 7,000 feet before stabilizing.
Israeli officials and passengers said the captain, an Indian national, was able to fight off his co-pilot and unlock the cockpit door. Witnesses recounted how a group of passengers and crew members then stormed the cockpit and subdued the co-pilot.
Two off-duty pilots then took control of the plane and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. There were 174 people on board, Israeli officials said. Most of the passengers later boarded a replacement FlyDubai plane and were flown to Ben Gurion International Airport, arriving Wednesday night.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker, whose name has not been released, was born in Oman and holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Netanyahu told CBS News he was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia.
"He'll be, I assume, moved very quickly to Dubai," Netanyahu told CBS News, adding that Israeli authorities will "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."
A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the pilot to the UAE for questioning.
Asked if he thought the incident could have stemmed from a mental health issue and not an act of terrorism, Netanyahu said, "it could be, I don't know, we'll find out soon."
"We've had signs that Iran, and particularly through its proxies, was intending to heighten terrorist attacks against Israel and Israeli nationals abroad," Netanyahu added. "But I think it's too early to say whether there was Iranian collusion here. I think we'll find out, won't take a long time."
No definitive motive for the stabbing has been determined by authorities. An Israeli security official previously told CBS News that investigators were looking into the possibility that the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," FlyDubai said in its own statement. It urged "all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."

The newest Windows 11 version 26H2 update has begun rolling out to millions of users worldwide, with some of them commenting that the latest iteration has introduced some optimizations regarding memory usage. Unfortunately, if you only have 8GB of RAM installed, then you’re probably excluded.
It appears that Microsoft hasn’t quite stuck with its promises of making Windows 11 more memory efficient for systems equipped with 8GB of memory . On Reddit , user “shutter_singh” has shown that RAM usage has decreased by 2GB after installing the latest update, but here’s the catch. If you look at the post below, his system is equipped with 48GB RAM, so it’s highly unlikely that a 2GB reduction will make or break his Windows 11 experience.
On the flipside, another Redditor with the handle “HenryDaGodzilla,” says that there was no change in the RAM usage after updating to version 26H2, and that’s probably because he’s using a Windows 11 system equipped with 8GB RAM instead of 48GB, with the former consuming a whopping 96 percent (7.4GB) of total system memory. On X, @SoyITPro notes that with the same update, his RAM consumption reduced from 9.1GB to 7.5GB.
However, he shares his Task Manager screenshot, revealing that he’s running 32GB of RAM, making it two instances where the Windows 11 26H2 update is benefiting systems with a higher memory count. Looking at these differences, it’s clear that Microsoft has the right approach when it comes to optimizing Windows 11, but the company should be laser-focused on ensuring that 8GB computers can run the operating system fluidly.

articles.content_orig:
A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China , making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week.
Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone …
Rising costs have seen overall sales of new smartphones in China decline 17% year on year since July, according to Counterpoint Research’s China Weekly Smartphone Sell-Out Tracker. However, the firm reports that this trend was reversed by the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro.
During the first three days of its sales (which accounted for only three days in Week 38), the iPhone 18 Pro series recorded 12% YoY growth compared with the iPhone sales. The strong initial performance helped Apple move into the No. 1 spot in sales in Week 38, with a 33% share of China’s smartphone market.
Counterpoint suggests there are three reasons underlying the popularity of the new model.
First, the delayed launch of the base iPhone 18. Because Apple has launched the two iPhone 18 Pro models well ahead of the standard model, some may have decided to upgrade to the premium version rather than wait.
Second, rising prices across all premium smartphones have led to consumers being willing to pay higher prices than would previously have been the case. Apple has absorbed some of the increased component costs, making the iPhone 18 Pro comparatively better value.
Third is what Counterpoint describes as “aggressive channel support,” generally meaning heavy advertising and promotions by retailers and carriers.

articles.title_orig: Ex-frat leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
articles.title_zh: Ex-frat leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
articles.content_orig:
Flagstaff — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge.
Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house.
An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state's legal limit for drivers 21 and over.
Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez's sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said.
Martinez's parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, CBS Phoenix affiliate KPHO-TV reported .
Eslick was the fraternity's pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members.
The hearing began with testimony from five of Eslick's friends and family members who attested to his character while warning about the dangers of fraternity culture, KPHO noted.
"While trying to teach my children these things, I realized I failed to teach him or explain to them, and in those gaps, toxic influence and toxic communities have stepped in," said Cody Eslick, Carter's father.
Carter Eslick apologized to Martinez's family, KPHO said.
"I am so incredibly deeply sorry for the events that happened on Jan. 31, and I take full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual," Eslick said. "And if I had known that one day somebody's life could be in my hands, there is no way in hell I would have ever looked that way."
Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family.
"My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss," Barker said in a statement.
Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it.
Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn't meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can't use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed.
The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez's death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter.

articles.title_orig: Britain and France Give Up Landmark Migrant Agreement
articles.title_zh: Britain and France Give Up Landmark Migrant Agreement
articles.content_orig:
Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems
UK politics live – latest updates
The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France , which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.
The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026.
The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey.
Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place.
It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from.
NGOs such as Medical Justice have condemned the trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisation Samusocial , which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force.
Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed.
In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. We just hope the UK doesn’t make a worse agreement with a new country.”

Photon Matrix Lab says it expects to produce up to 5,000 devices a month initially, and then increase production capacity next year
People have been trying to fend off mosquitoes for thousands of years – using methods ranging from physical barriers to chemical insecticides – but a Chinese start-up is now taking pre-orders on a hi-tech solution that uses lidar detection and lasers to zap them out of the air.
Photon Matrix Lab, based in Changzhou, in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, said it expected initial monthly production of the device – which became a breakout hit in overseas crowdfunding – to be between 3,000 and 5,000 units.
Lawrence Leng, the firm’s sales director, said the first batch was expected to ship later this month.

articles.title_orig: What we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in September
articles.title_zh: What we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in September
articles.content_orig:
Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
I was sideswiped by Giada Scodellaro’s Ruins, Child . A brilliant, strange book that challenged me in the most exhilarating way, with its fractured language and dream-cinema visions, the sense it bestowed of walking through a corridor full of echoes. Echoes of a less elliptical but no-less political kind haunt Jordy Rosenberg’s astounding Night Night Fawn . I guess you could call it a family novel? But it’s at least as much about fascism as it is about the family – as well as about unsettling linkages between the two. And for horrors and rage in a nonfiction register, Jonas Marvin’s The Breaking of the English Working Class is an indispensable – and beautifully written – essay on decades of structural, economic and psychic violence. The feeling it provoked in me brought to mind John Berger’s phrase “undefeated despair”.
The Rouse by China Miéville is published by Picador (£35). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.
I was totally immersed in Whale Fall by Elizabeth O’Connor, a beautifully written story describing a short time in the life of a young woman and her fishing community on an island off the coast of Wales in the 1930s. The simplicity of this tale is underpinned with intriguing moral issues when two anthropologists visit the island to study the lives and history of the islanders. The book is the most poetic I’ve read in a while.
I’ve enjoyed so many books recently. Two I now claim as favourites of all time. The first is Beloved by Toni Morrison . Incredibly late to the party because I was resistant to reading her again having had such a hard time with Sula. But Beloved, in my opinion, is the perfect novel. The second is Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo, one of the founding texts of the Latin American tradition of magical realism. It was hard work but so enjoyable, a reminder that challenging can be fun and that it’s possible to tell a story in a variety of ways. Last, I want to mention The Bridge of San Luis Rey by Thornton Wilder. I’ve only just finished it, so coherent feelings are still working themselves out, but in the mix I know there is admiration, pleasure, something life affirming and something ineffable sparked by the religious elements of the novel. I’m almost certain it’s going to join the others as one of my favourites. I’m having a great run.
The Recovery House by Derek Owusu is published by Merky Books (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.
In the day, Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin, a giant ship of a book which, at nearly a thousand pages, will probably steer me through the remains of 2026. In the night, when I cannot sleep, I do as I always do around the date of my birthday: a re-read of all of Jean Rhys. With her, I am on the moonlit deck of the ship and we watch the darkness of a deep sea rush by. For sanity, The Practice of Not Thinking by Ryunosuke Koike: the antidote to botched CBT therapy. For inspiration, For Now by Eileen Myles, concerning the loss of part of their archive and the struggle to hold on to a rent controlled apartment of 40 years. And My Life on the Road by Gloria Steinem. Of course.
after newsletter promotion
If anyone is in a mood to have their psyches calmed and their reading synapses restored, then The Last Chronicle of Barset by Anthony Trollope is the cat’s pyjamas. I was nodding my head recently when Marlon James was saying somewhere that he rated Trollope above Dickens. Not that D is any slouch. I am rereading a book I read for work, and now again just because it’s so excellently done, Army Life in a Black Regiment , by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Emerson said it was a masterpiece by a writer not known for writing masterpieces(!) The Penguin Classics reissue in the late 1990s also has his correspondence with Emily Dickinson and an account of his one meeting with her, revelatory on many levels. She spoke as she wrote. I was also very admiring of a little book of poems by Kayleigh Jayshree called Mango and Starblush , which Miss Dickinson might have called true poems.

articles.title_orig: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
articles.title_zh: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
articles.content_orig:
"I'm very shocked" - College students react to Cornell University rape investigation
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault.
When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault.
The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence.
Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing.
"Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence."
The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system".
How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case.
What we know about Cornell rape investigation
Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically.
The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported.
"These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate."
Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case.
Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. I n a statement , external , the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus.
Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled.
Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy.
Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached.
One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation.
"Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said.
Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault.
"For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials.
While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting.
Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration.
"I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said.
The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment.
University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations.
"The secrecy of the process, it prevents other students from knowing about it. It prevents witnesses from coming forward," she said.
Michael Diamondstein, a Pennsylvania attorney who has represented those accused of sexual misconduct on college campuses, said the secrecy helps protect both the victim and the accused.
"I think when you compare it to what they would face in a courtroom, it's much easier for students and much safer for students. Their name isn't put out there. The news media doesn't get them," he said.
Cornell students have criticised the university's handling of the woman's claims. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the names of the accused under the headline: "Cornell won't, we will."
In a statement, the college said that federal privacy law "prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individualâ¯students" so it cannot "make a public statement on any other disciplinary response".
Many advocates say there is merit to universities investigating sexual assault complaints separately from the criminal justice system. Prosecuting sexual assault cases is notoriously difficult - a recent systematic review found that less than 10% of sexual assault cases yielded convictions. In a criminal trial, a prosecutor must convince a jury "beyond reasonable doubt" that the accused is guilty. But in a campus tribunal, the burden of proof is lower.
Under Title IX, the university is also required to offer solutions that local law enforcement cannot, like ensuring a student is not in the same class as their alleged abuser while the investigation is ongoing and offering homework extensions, said Scheinblum-Brewer.
This is one of several reasons why victims and advocates for survivors say there are benefits to having two separate avenues, through the university and the criminal justice system.
For Mary, after her case was dropped by the police, pursuing her assault claim through Title IX became the only way for her alleged rapist to face repercussions: an expulsion from college.

articles.title_orig: PS5 emulation is suddenly making big strides on PC
articles.title_zh: PS5 emulation is suddenly making big strides on PC
articles.content_orig:
For a long time, PC gamers could access many PlayStation 5 games only if the publisher invested in a bespoke port (something Sony has recently said it will be scaling back ). Now, though, rapid advancements in PS5 emulators and other tools are making recent PlayStation titles increasingly playable on generic PCs.
SharpEmu was the first of these emulators, advancing from a “very early alpha stage” in May to a current state that can “load the eboot.bin of real games, execute native CPU instructions, and partially handle GPU-related functionality.” The most recent release boasts 10 tested games that reach a “playable” state , including six that developer CursedIfElse says are “fully playable at 60 fps.” That includes simple 2D games like Tetris Forever but also 3D titles like Astro Bot and the PS5 Demon’s Souls remaster running at playable frame rates.
“SharpEmu has prioritized hardware accuracy from the very beginning, and we’re finally starting to see that investment pay off,” CursedIfElse wrote on social media this week . “It was built completely from scratch, and this is how far we’ve come.”
Amid that SharpEmu progress, fellow PS5 emulator KytyPS5 launched its first public version last week . The major expansion of PS4-focused emulator Kyty “can boot 2D games and a selection of 3D games, including titles built with Unreal Engine 4/5, Unity, and custom engines,” according to its GitHub page .
An extensive compatibility list for KytyPS5 already shows 134 titles with “controllable gameplay” on the new emulator, though many of those still include reports of persistent, game-breaking bugs. But you can already find YouTube footage of PS5 titles like Astro’s Playroom and Demon’s Souls running quite capably under the emulator.
On top of those more traditional emulators, AnyPS5 might be the most interesting effort to get PS5 games running on PC. The self-described “tool for automatic executables porting” works kind of like Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit , relinking a PS5 game’s original x86 game code directly to native executable instructions that can run on PC. That puts the effort somewhere between direct static decompilation of a game’s source code and more complete emulation of the entire PS5 environment.
AnyPS5 is still in its early days, but already has about 76 percent of system libraries and 50 percent GPU shader instructions fully supported, according to its developers. That’s enough to get simple games like Dreaming Sarah to a “playable state” and has led to proof-of-concept footage of the PS5 edition of Dead Cells running as a native PC executable.
We’re still probably a long way off from the day when a solid majority of the PS5 library can be ably run on PC hardware. Still, the recent burst in activity and compatibility progress should give PC players hope that day will be coming eventually.

articles.title_orig: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
articles.title_zh: Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
articles.content_orig:
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
"We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release , which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board.  Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

articles.title_orig: A top QB showdown and a historic anniversary: 5 things to know from the NFL this week
articles.title_zh: A top QB showdown and a historic anniversary: 5 things to know from the NFL this week
articles.content_orig:
Three weeks into the NFL season, we’re already seeing some familiar storylines, some huge surprises and plenty of history being made.
The Houston Texans are 0-3 – again – while the Las Vegas Raiders are sitting at a surprising 3-0. Joe Burrow and Trevor Lawrence are renewing a rivalry this week that goes all the way back to college; some of the NFL’s biggest stars are putting up ridiculous numbers, and Monday night in New Orleans will mark the anniversary of one of the most memorable games in NFL history.
Here are five things to watch in Week 4.
Well, this is déjà vu for Texans fans. Another 0-3 start.
Last season, the Texans became just the seventh team ever to make the playoffs after starting 0-3, and they’ve actually done it twice — in 2025 and 2018. But no team has ever lost its first three games and then made the playoffs in back-to-back seasons.
And only one team has ever started 0-4 and made the playoffs. That was the 1992 San Diego Chargers, who started 0-4 but then won 11 of their final 12 games.
Do the Texans have that kind of run in them?
Well, they would have to start finding a way to block and run the ball, but their upcoming schedule isn’t that difficult. Their next seven games are against the Dallas Cowboys, Tennessee Titans, Jacksonville Jaguars in London, New York Giants, Los Angeles Chargers, Cleveland Browns and then the Indianapolis Colts at home.
If Houston can go 5-2 during that stretch and get to 5-5, the Texans would be well on their way to salvaging the season. And with the AFC South just 3-9 collectively, chasing down a division title is certainly not out of the question despite another terrible start.
On the other side of things, Raider Nation is riding high after yet another thrilling win.
The Raiders are 3-0 for the first time since 2021 and are actually the first team ever to start a season 3-0 after drafting a quarterback No. 1 overall.
But Fernando Mendoza has had nothing to do with the wins.
Instead, 38-year-old Kirk Cousins has found the fountain of youth!
Inside Fernando Mendoza’s record-setting quest
Cousins has been fantastic, throwing three touchdowns in each of the Raiders’ first three games. Fans were hoping Cousins would play well after he reunited with Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak, who was his offensive coordinator with the Minnesota Vikings when Cousins had some of the best seasons of his career. Right now, Cousins is tied with San Francisco 49ers QB Brock Purdy for the most passing touchdowns this season.
Now, the Raiders’ wins so far have come against the lowly Miami Dolphins, Chargers and New Orleans Saints, so this 3-0 start may turn out to be a bit of a mirage.
But if Las Vegas can beat the 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs at home Sunday, that would be a huge statement win – and give the Raiders their first 4-0 start since 2002.
We have a showdown between former No. 1 overall picks Sunday in Cincinnati as Joe Burrow and the Bengals host Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars.
This is a game Lawrence will certainly be motivated for because he has never beaten Burrow — even dating back to college.
Burrow and LSU beat Lawrence and Clemson in the national championship game in January 2020. Burrow has also beaten Lawrence in both of their head-to-head matchups in the NFL.
But if Burrow wants to once again get the better of Lawrence, he’d better already be winning late.
Burrow is 1-34 when trailing in the final eight minutes of regulation.
If you drafted Jahmyr Gibbs, Jaxon Smith-Njigba or Josh Allen in your fantasy league, you’re likely off to a great start because all three are scoring at a historic pace.
Gibbs was the consensus No. 1 overall fantasy pick, and he’s lived up to the hype, scoring six touchdowns in the Detroit Lions’ first three games. He’s just the fifth running back ever to do that to start a season.
JSN, meanwhile, has been incredible for the Seahawks, leading the NFL in both receiving yards and touchdowns. He’s had at least 120 receiving yards and a touchdown in each game, joining Hall of Famer Jerry Rice as the only receiver in NFL history to do that in each of the first three games of a season.
With two more rushing touchdowns in Sunday’s win over the Chargers, Allen became the first quarterback in NFL history with multiple rushing touchdowns in three consecutive games.
The Buffalo QB already has the most rushing touchdowns ever by a quarterback with 85. That puts him tied for 17th on the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list. And Allen is still only 30 years old!
His Bills will look for a 4-0 start when they host the New England Patriots on Sunday.
Monday night will be an emotional one in New Orleans as the Saints commemorate the 20th anniversary of their return to the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina.
On September 25, 2006, the Saints beat the Atlanta Falcons 23-3 in their first game back at the Superdome following the storm.
Steve Gleason’s blocked punt, which was recovered for a Saints touchdown, remains one of the most iconic moments in franchise – and arguably NFL – history. The moment is now immortalized with a statue outside the Superdome.
That game became known as the “Domecoming” or “Rebirth” game and served as a powerful symbol of recovery and resilience for the city of New Orleans and the entire Gulf Coast region following the devastation of Hurricane Katrina.
Twenty years later, the Falcons and Saints will meet again on Monday night.
Both teams enter the matchup at 1-2.

NEW YORK â The sweetness of summer is so gone it can be hard to remember. Its memory is subsumed by the earlier nightfall, the zipping of a jacket, trees giving up their leaves in surrender to the coming cold and, if youâre the Boston Red Sox, the relentless might of the New York Yankees. The 37 midsummer games when the Red Sox saved their season and won in ways that were almost laughable are now dried flowers in an album, a poor placeholder for what once was.Â
Can you remember? Maybe not if you saw the Yankeesâwithout Aaron Judgeâsteamroll Boston in a wild-card sweep, 9â0 in Game 1 Tuesday and 9â2 in Game 2 Wednesday. And it wasnât that close.
âThat,â New York manager Aaron Boone says, âwas about as good as we can play. I just told the guys, âIf we play like that, we can beat anybody.ââ
The Red Soxâ season ended spectacularly poorly, which is to say it was a matching bookend to the year. Itâs a tragicomedy in three acts: 32â46, 32â5 and 23â26 in which they were the worst hitting team in baseball for the last month. The anomaly was those 37 games of summer bliss.
The way the season ended, the Red Sox must question their offensive depth. Certainly, it was no match against the firepower and depth of the Judge-less Yankees.
Rarely do playoff games devolve into ugly mismatches, but thatâs what happened over two games. The Yankees knocked the spirit out of what was, during its heyday, a feisty Boston team. Willson Contreras didnât cover first base while his shortstop laid out for a liner and he didnât stretch for a throw from catcher Adley Rutschman on a third-strike wild pitch, the spark to the flame of six runs in the sixth. Manager Chad Tracy repeated his mistake of pulling his starter to ask Erik Miller to be a shutdown lefty relieverâwhile lefties are batting .533 against Miller this month. Jazz Chisholm Jr. stole second base standing up with a six-run lead. Rutschman threw a ball into center field on a stolen base by Spencer Jones. It was about as anticlimactic a series as you could find.
CODY BELLINGER THREE-RUN HOMER IT'S 8-1 YANKEES! pic.twitter.com/gUQC8CJQb9
While the Red Sox were left to question where they are on the winning curve, the Yankees found their new voice without Judge. The Bronx Bombers looked like the Rays, their next opponent in the American League division series. Game 2 marked the first postseason game in franchise history in which they sprayed 12 singles around the field and stole four bases. Throw in two run-scoring productive outs and a perfectly executed bunt and New York showcased speed and athleticism that give them another ramp to victory if Judge is not recovered from his calf injury in time for the ALDS.
The Rays will present a different, better challenge to the Yankees than Boston. But again, the Yankees have much more offensive depth and more elite stuff in the rotation. Cam Schlittler and Max Fried, allowing one run in 12 1/3 combined innings, never allowed Boston momentum, constantly keeping Red Sox hitters off balance. Brilliantly mixing his pitches, Fried hit 23 different speeds between 73 mph and 98 mph.Â
Tampa Bay won the season series against New York, 7â6, but was outscored, 54â45. The Rays are an opportunistic team that doesnât strike out, but they were 12th in the majors in runs per game. They prefer to play a series with soccer scores to take out New York. And that may be their one path, whereas the Yankees, as they showed Boston, have many avenues to victory.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

articles.title_zh: The Cornell Rape Investigation: Five Takeaways
articles.content_orig:
A detailed timeline has emerged in the case of the ex-Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped by seven male fraternity members while on drugs at a house party, shedding new light on how she decided to push for justice.
The young woman, identified as Jane Doe, is suing Cornell and the seven members of the Ivy League school's Chi Phi fraternity house, alleging that she was pressured into taking ketamine and sexually assaulted for hours on October 19, 2024, at the Chi Phi fraternity house party in Ithaca, New York. No arrests have been made in connection to the case, and the local district attorney has said he is reopening the case in light of the civil suit.
More than 1,000 pages of documents in the case– including text messages between Doe and some of the men accused of being involved in the assault, interviews, and photographs– collected during Cornell's internal Title IX proceedings were obtained by The New York Times . They capture Doe's apparent state of mind during the three weeks from the night in question to the day she reported the incident to the university police on Nov. 8, 2024.
The documents paint a picture of the sophomore woman who struggled to grapple with what allegedly unfolded at the frat house party, even reassuring her alleged abusers in text messages, before she concluded what happened was "not consensual," the newspaper reports.
Attorneys for at least three of the men, whose images are plastered across social media, have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing, while others have not made public statements.
A detailed timeline has emerged in the case of the ex-Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped by seven male fraternity members while on drugs at a house party, shedding new light on how she decided to push for justice (Getty Images)
Doe's roommates told the school's investigators that she arrived home around 11:15 a.m. the morning of Oct. 20, still wearing her "big boots and small dress" from the night before, according to the documents obtained by the Times .
She reportedly told her roommates she had taken ketamine and had sex with multiple men. A roommate told investigators that Doe appeared to be "in shock" and was "not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying."
Another roommate told investigators that Doe had not yet used the words "rape or assault."
Doe reached out to her "big sister" at Cornell's Tri Delta sorority, her mentor-like figure, and said rumors swirled on campus that she was a "slut." The big sister reportedly told investigators that she recalled Doe adding, "Unfortunately, they are true," with a laugh.
"I could tell that — just from personal experiences — that what she was going through was that she had not yet processed what had happened," the big sister reportedly said.
One of the men named in the lawsuit, Jonathan Newell, reportedly texted Doe on Oct. 21, two days after the party. "I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night," he allegedly wrote.
Newell reportedly said that he and Matthew Ingalls, Doe's friend who brought her to the party, felt bad for being too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand."

Doe reportedly replied with a reassuring message. "At the end of the day non [sic] of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt," she reportedly wrote.
On October 22, Doe reportedly arranged to see a doctor at Cornell Health after contracting a urinary tract infection. She reportedly told the doctor that it was contracted "in a traumatic way" and was allegedly advised to "go to therapy."
An attorney for Ingalls declined to comment when approached for comment by the Times . Newell's lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.
On October 23, Doe texted Ingalls saying "everyone knows" and that the rumors were "RUINING my life temporarily." She reportedly told him that all she could do was "sleep and cry all day." Ingalls reportedly replied by comforting her, and said that she did not have "anything to be ashamed of."
Doe, meanwhile, reportedly told a concerned roommate: "If anyone asks about this, say it didn't happen."
The roommate reportedly told investigators: "As the days went on, I think she kind of came to realize that it was something bad. And that she didn't really enjoy her time there."
Approximately one week later, with posts swirling about the party online, Doe sent Ingalls one from a student forum accusing Chi Phi of gang rape.
Ingalls reportedly called the allegation "ridiculous" and said, "I'm gonna report that."
Doe then found another post about the party and the alleged assault.
"Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?" someone reportedly posted.
Attorneys for at least three of the men, whose images are plastered across social media, have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing, while others have not made public statements (Getty)
"They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore," another reportedly said. "Report them."
After reading the posts, Doe reportedly told investigators it was "the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted."
Doe's roommates reportedly told investigators that toward the end of the month, her perception of what happened to her had shifted.
In a phone call with Ingalls on October 28 that one roommate overheard, she reportedly told him: "How could you let this happen?"
Doe had reportedly been sexually assaulted before, the roommate told investigators. "I'd have conversations and she would describe a part of what happened and I would tell her that that is what could be classified as rape," the roommate said.
Ingalls initially told Doe that she was welcome at the fraternity's upcoming Halloween party. "chi phi is your house and you are welcome here," he reportedly texted her.

"thank u i really appreciate that <3 i'll bring my cigs tomorrow," Doe reportedly replied.
Doe later received a phone call from Chi Phi's president, who is not among the accused, according to the Times , where he disinvited her from the Halloween party. He reportedly told her that it was for her own good, according to the Times .
"I knew this was going to happen," Doe reportedly texted Ingalls. "The woman will always get the short end of the stick. Yall aren't my friends. Yall are covering your asses."
Doe characterizes the events of Oct. 19 as "not consensual" in text messages reportedly sent to Newell in early November.
She appears to conclude by this point that what happened was assault.
"Let's be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn't know anyone in the room," she reportedly texted Newell, using slang for ketamine.
One of her only memories from that night was doing ketamine off of his genitals "in front of everyone like a sex doll/worker," she reportedly continued in the text to Newell.
According to the documents, she requested a rape kit from an emergency room in Ithaca on Nov. 7, before making the report to Cornell's University police department the following day.
The university has come under fire for its response to the incident, with Doe alleging that the school failed to protect her or adequately punish those responsible.

Last week, President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. It's their second meeting this year, following the May summit in Beijing. This visit, the stakes were even higher .
We have learned about security incidents from nearly every major AI company, American and Chinese, built on both open and closed models. The leading AI labs are openly debating whether to pace their frontier model development, and the government is working out what role it plays in that decision.
I spent four years as Secretary of Commerce focused intently on America’s economic, technological, and security competition with China—instituting first-of-its-kind export controls on the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China to protect our national security, and leading implementation of the CHIPS Act to onshore chip manufacturing. I also created the AI Safety Institute so we could accelerate our AI development responsibly and safely. I have sat across the table from China, and I have an understanding of how they think about AI.
I believe AI companies are right to want to pace the frontier. But we need to stay ahead of China while we pace, because a world where China leads the global AI competition threatens America’s interests.
The challenge is this: We need to outcompete China on the technology itself, while also working with China on addressing the risks posed by AI. Competition and cooperation are often in tension, but the stakes are too high in this case to pick only one.
China has its own reasons to take AI safety seriously. The Chinese Minister of State Security recently said publicly that the greatest risk advanced AI poses to China is the risk it poses to the stability of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Beijing is no more interested in powerful AI systems wreaking socio-political havoc than Washington is; both countries have incentives to align on certain safety standards or even just a shared understanding of AI risks. It is in neither country’s interest for companies to lose control of their AI systems or for AI to be used to create bioweapons by rogue actors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement of a possible AI dialogue with Chinese counterparts after his meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng is a tangible sign that China sees at least some space for cooperation here.
I would argue that now is the moment to fully establish that dialogue and keep the momentum going. We should do this by convening experts from both countries. I’m well aware that we’d be foolish to trust People's Republic of China (PRC) leaders. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t try. It just means we need to develop verification mechanisms to ensure agreements work even in the absence of trust.
Even if we don’t reach agreement on a shared set of standards, starting a dialogue and opening those lines of communication are critical—just as we did in 2008 during the financial crisis, when it was in our mutual benefit to coordinate. And we spent decades during the Cold War in careful, ongoing dialogue with the Soviet Union about nuclear arms control because the risks to both countries were enormous. During that time we developed zero-trust methods to verify arms control agreements even while locked in an adversarial relationship.
None of that changes the need to vigilantly and continuously update our controls as technology changes so China can’t access our most sophisticated compute in ways that threaten our national security. That includes continuously updating our export controls on leading-edge chips, addressing the risks of China accessing controlled compute remotely in data centers around the world, and cracking down on diversion of technology that is controlled.
We also need to tighten remaining gaps in our semiconductor manufacturing equipment controls so China can less capably obtain tools to manufacture powerful chips at scale and service their pre-existing equipment. That work has to happen with our Dutch, Japanese, and German allies and partners who manufacture and service this chipmaking equipment.
Finally, the U.S. government should put a greater burden on the AI companies to take adversarial distillation much more seriously. Distillation —coordinated, industrial-scale efforts by AI labs to train their weaker models on the outputs of frontier models—has become a significant issue in the past year. Anthropic has attributed more than 16 million Claude exchanges to distillation campaigns, and has estimated that over 3 million of these distillation campaigns can be traced back to China’s Moonshot AI  (the company behind China’s version of ChatGPT, Kimi) along with other Chinese AI labs like Alibaba and DeepSeek. Moonshot, for instance, was later caught forwarding user prompts to Claude to answer and feeding those answers back through Kimi.
China has certainly indigenized much of its AI stack, something Xi publicly made a priority in his Made in China 2025 plan, many years before the U.S. government was talking openly about chips or models. And China has made progress on this plan. But it is clear to many that China’s most competitive models, to some degree, are ripping off American ones. American AI labs should be allocating even greater amounts of their money and compute towards finding and exposing this kind of activity so that policymakers—and the public—can adapt accordingly.
The risks and benefits of AI are enormous, something more and more Americans have come to realize as AI advances more quickly than we previously thought possible. There is much to do on AI safety at home, to ensure our society and economy are resilient to the dramatic changes AI will bring. But I also know that safe deployment of AI is only possible if we successfully manage our relationship with China—both by maintaining our technological lead and working towards collaboration.

articles.title_orig: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.title_zh: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.content_orig:
What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.
She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.
The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.
One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.
Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.
Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
Why the death penalty is on the rise in US
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.
The DPI says lethal injection has the highÂ­est rate of botched exeÂ­cuÂ­tions.
An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.
In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia's Prabowo appoints new foreign minister
articles.title_zh: Indonesia's Prabowo appoints new foreign minister
articles.content_orig:
The reshuffle comes less than three weeks after President Prabowo Subianto sacked Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa as finance minister and appointed his deputy as his replacement.
A file photo of Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto during the State of the Nation Address on Aug 14, 2026. (File photo: AFP/Bay Ismoyo)
JAKARTA: In his biggest Cabinet reshuffle to date, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Thursday (Oct 1) has appointed new foreign and industry ministers, as well as new coordinating ministers over several portfolios.
Arrmanatha Nasir was named as his new foreign minister, moving up from his role as deputy foreign minister. The career diplomat replaces Sugiono, who is now Coordinating Minister for Human Development and Culture.
Golkar party politician Muhammad Sarmuji was named as the Minister of Industry, replacing Agus Gumiwang Kartasasmita.
Presidential Chief of Staff Dudung Abdurachman will now serve as the Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs while Bahlil Lahadalia has been appointed the Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition, a new position in the Cabinet.
Bahlil continues in his role as the Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources.
In total, the changes involved 10 ministerial and deputy ministerial appointments, as well as eight other senior leaders of agencies and the police force. All 18 were sworn in at the presidential palace in Jakarta on Thursday afternoon.
Speaking to reporters after the swearing-in ceremony, Arrmanatha said Sugiono has run the foreign ministry very well, and he will continue his predecessor’s programmes.
One of Indonesia’s foreign policy goals is to become a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for the 2029-2030 term, Arrmanatha said.
“Our bid for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2029–2030 term reaffirms Indonesia's commitment to active participation in creating a safer, more stable world,” he said.
“It also demonstrates our confidence in and emphasis on the importance of multilateralism and we will continue to use this candidacy as an opportunity to push for reform of the multilateral system.”
On Thursday, Prabowo also replaced the country's police chief , a role currently held by Listyo Sigit Prabowo, with the head of the National Narcotics Agency Suyudi Ario Seto. Listyo was then appointed as head of the Executive Office of the President in Thursday’s reshuffle.
The changes to Prabowo’s Cabinet come less than three weeks after the president sacked former finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and appointed his deputy Suahasil Nazara as his replacement on Sep 14.
O n Thursday, Prabowo also appointed Drajad Hari Wibowo as the Deputy Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs, Nurkholisoh Ibnu Aman as the Deputy Minister of Finance and Luky Alfirman as the Deputy Minister of Finance.
Muhammad Saleh Mustafa was appointed the Deputy Minister of Agriculture while Irwan Meilano will serve as Deputy Minister of Marine Affairs and Fisheries.

RIO DE JANEIRO — As Brazilians prepare to vote in the first round of the presidential election Sunday, they're weighing sharp differences between the top candidates on security , foreign policy and the environment . But they're also thinking about kitchen table issues.
And if you really want to know how Brazilians feel about the economy, look no further than how often picanha , the country's prized cut of beef, is on the table.
When left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was campaigning for his current role four years ago, he told voters they would be able to afford picanha again if he were elected. At the time, Brazil's economy was still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic.
Picanha , or a top sirloin cap steak, is a marker of prosperity in this beef-loving country.
Lula is now running for reelection in what polls suggest is a tight race with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro . Lula's economic record is among the many issues under scrutiny by voters — and a recent survey found that only 10% of Brazilians feel their income has grown faster than the cost of living in the past year.
Marcella Pirozzi, 44, the co-owner of a Rio de Janeiro barbecue company, says these days she only tries to sell picanha in wealthy parts of the city. In poorer areas, people are "more conservative" about their spending, she says. "We don't get hired to cater events very often due to meat prices."
At his butcher shop on Rio's working-class north side, 37-year-old Arthur Guedes says he's also scaled back how much picanha he expects to sell in recent years. Instead, he's focusing on a more accessible product: hamburger patties.
A woman buys meat at the São Paulo Municipal Market in downtown São Paulo, Brazil. The South American country will hold elections on Sunday. Luis Robayo/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
After Lula took office, a burst of public spending caused economic growth to speed up, though it's now slowing. In the first three years of his term, average wages grew more than inflation . But household indebtedness also shot up , thanks to factors like a boom in sports gambling , easy access to credit lines, and high interest rates.
By this June, Brazilian households were spending 26.6% of their income on non-mortgage debt payments, according to the central bank.
Some analysts say a concept from the United States now applies in Brazil: that of a " vibecession ." The term was first used in former President Joe Biden's administration to describe an economy that is not technically in recession, but feels unaffordable.
University of São Paulo economist Laura Carvalho argues the phrase is apt. She says the gap between the economic data and how it's perceived could come from Brazilians making mental comparisons with an earlier period when Lula was president, in the 2000s. Brazil's economy boomed dramatically, and many families could afford items like refrigerators and air travel for the first time.
In contrast, today's economy is suffering from price shocks that didn't exist back then, Carvalho said: "the pandemic, and then the war in Ukraine, and now, with the Iran war." Trump's heavy tariffs on Brazil have also taken an economic toll .
Brazil's voter worries about the cost of living are part of a worldwide phenomenon, according to Carvalho.
"You have incumbents everywhere that are suffering the effects of the price increases of the different shocks," she said. "People look at the price increase and they blame whoever is in government."
Bolsonaro, a senator for Rio de Janeiro, is playing up the idea that basic staples have become unaffordable. He published a video of himself denouncing prices in the supermarket, making sure to name-check picanha.
But he has not given much detail about his own economic proposals. He broadly argues that cutting taxes and government spending will boost growth. One of Bolsonaro's top advisers has praised the policies of libertarian Argentine President Javier Milei, which have reduced inflation but seen poverty rise in recent months.
Lula, for his part, has downplayed concerns that Brazil's national debt might be getting unsustainable. He's announced new measures in recent days meant to address household indebtedness, like a debt restructuring program and ban on online betting.
Guedes, the butcher shop owner, says that only days before the election, he still hasn't decided how to vote.
"I don't see clear strategies from the candidates for how to improve the country," he says.
Pirozzi has made up her mind. She says she's "ready for a change" and will vote for Bolsonaro.
